title: Russian Drones Destroy Indian-Run Kusum Pharma Plant in Ukraine, One Killed
excerpt: The main structure of the Kusum Group's Sumy facility was largely destroyed in Sunday's strike, which killed one worker and injured several others. The company puts its losses at at least ₹400 crore.
body:
• Russian drones struck the Kusum Group's pharmaceutical plant in Sumy, Ukraine, on Sunday morning, largely destroying the main structure. One worker was killed and several were injured.
  • The Indian-run company, led by Rajeev Gupta, estimates its losses at at least ₹400 crore. Its Delhi office declined to comment on the attack.
  • This is Kusum's second major wartime blow in Ukraine: a company warehouse in Kyiv was destroyed by a direct Russian drone hit in April 2025.
  • President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the attack, which came amid a wider barrage that also hit sites in Kyiv and Dnipro.

A pharmaceutical manufacturing plant in Ukraine belonging to India's Kusum Group was largely destroyed in a Russian drone attack on Sunday morning, killing one worker and injuring several others, according to local officials and reports. Visuals from the site showed a huge plume of smoke rising from the facility in the city of Sumy, in northeastern Ukraine, with the main structure of the plant mostly reduced to rubble.

Officials warned that the casualty and injury figures could change as rescue and damage-assessment operations continue. The plant had kept operating through more than three years of full-scale war — making its destruction the most serious blow yet to an Indian enterprise with deep roots in Ukraine.

"They attacked an ordinary pharmaceutical warehouse in Sumy with drones. Tragically, one person was killed. My condolences to the family and loved ones."

— Volodymyr Zelensky, President of Ukraine

Context & Background

The Kusum Group began in 1994 as a distributor exporting Indian medicines to Ukraine. It is currently run by Indian national Rajeev Gupta and describes itself as a Ukrainian pharmaceutical company with Indian roots.

https://x.com/NDTVWorld/status/2106650737904386411

In 2002, the group stopped distributing medicines made by other companies and began marketing its own brands. It then moved into manufacturing, opening its first plant in India in 2007 and a facility in Sumy in 2009, followed by two more manufacturing facilities in India — in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, and Pithampur, Madhya Pradesh. The company says its units are WHO-GMP certified and PIC/S compliant.

The group manufactures more than 50 mostly generic products and sells them in over nine countries, with Ukraine, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and the Philippines among its principal markets. In 2023, Kusum said its Sumy plant employed more than 500 people and produced generic medicines across several therapeutic categories, including cardiology, gastroenterology, anti-inflammatory, hypotensive and paediatric medicines — with production continuing despite the war.

Impact & Analysis

The Sumy strike is not the first major wartime blow to Kusum's Ukrainian operations. In April 2025, a Kusum Group pharmaceutical warehouse in Kyiv was completely destroyed after a direct hit by a Russian drone. The company said the warehouse contained finished medicines, active pharmaceutical ingredients, excipients and newly installed production equipment, with damage estimated at about 1 billion Ukrainian hryvnias. No employees were injured in that attack.

This time the human cost is starker: one person killed and several injured, with the loss estimated at at least ₹400 crore. When contacted by phone, the Kusum Group's Delhi office declined to comment on the attack, and emailed queries remained unanswered at the time of publication.

The attack fits a broader pattern. Since the summer, Moscow has launched dozens of fast, relatively inexpensive jet-powered Shahed drones daily, and Ukrainian air-defence units have struggled because some interceptor drones were too slow to catch them. Industrial and civilian facilities in Sumy have repeatedly come under attack: on October 3, Russian forces struck civilian enterprises in the Kovpakivsky district with four guided bombs, and in August Ukraine's foreign ministry said Russian drone strikes damaged a Mondelēz International facility in the Sumy region, injuring several employees.

Diaspora Angle

Kusum is one of the most established Indian business success stories in Ukraine — a company that started by selling Indian medicines there in the 1990s and grew into a manufacturer employing hundreds of Ukrainians. Its Sumy plant at 54 Skriabyna Street was described by the company as one of Ukraine's modern pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities. The destruction of the plant is a reminder that Indian enterprises and the Indian diaspora's economic footprint in Ukraine remain exposed to the war's escalation, even as they continue to operate.

What's Next

Authorities are still assessing the full damage and final casualty figures at the Sumy site. Kusum has not yet issued a public statement on the strike. Meanwhile, Ukraine announced this week the first combat use of its domestically produced FP-7 ballistic missile, with an approximate range of 250 km, as Kyiv seeks to expand its long-range strike capability amid the continuing war.

nri_angle: An Indian-run pharmaceutical company that grew from exporting Indian medicines to Ukraine into a major local manufacturer has lost its flagship Ukrainian plant to the war, putting hundreds of Ukrainian jobs and an Indian business success story at risk.
